Q: How can I merge multiple lines into one line in Vim? A:

Or to join everything from the opening square bracket to the closing square bracket (assuming you have lots of these in your file) and leaving other lines intact,

:g/\[/,/\]/j

is quick and simple.

Q: I am getting this error when I add camera plug in A:

To work around this, you can add a dependency on androidx.concurrent:concurrent-futures to your own project.

The owners of androidx.camera:camera-core could work around this for their users by changing their dependency on concurrent-futures from implementation to api, since Gradle occasionally removes too many classes from the classpath when you use implementation.

Gradle could change that behavior, but that would likely be a big project.

The best hope for a general fix is likely for Java to stop producing an error in this case. (But it may still produce a warning, so it may remain better for builds to supply the missing class.)

Q: Remove leading space in xsl:when A:

Tests here suggest that the leading space is inserted by Word when the Citation is immediately preceded by text that is not whitespace.

e.g. if you insert the Citation at the beginning of a paragraph, it will look like

(Doe, 2026)

If you then insert "abc" at the beginning of the paragraph, you will see

abc(Doe, 2026)

but when you click the Citation's menu and "Update", you will see

abc (Doe, 2026)

In other words, the problem is not in the .xsl. You can verify that by choosing any other Referencing style and updating the citation, or to be completely sure, writing a .xsl that just returns (say) xyz to Word.

I don't think this is new behaviour - e.g., it seems to be the same in Word 2007.

A possible workaround might be to ensure that there is either a very thin space or a hidden space immediately before the Citation, e.g.

Some text (<very thin or hidden space>(Doe, 2026)).

That seems to work OK here but I haven't tried things that you may need to do such as print, convert to PDF and so on.

Incidentally, it doesn't seem to make any difference whether the citation is inserted in the usual way (where you get an "sdt" box with a menu and a CITATION field inside) or insert a CITATION field directly, with out the surrounding sdt.

Q: What is the best way to remember which function to use for which situation? A:

If you use something occasionally then it's impossible to remember all details.

If you use something few times a day then brain can remember it automatically.

Q: How to properly quote associate array subscripts in Bash? A:

IMO we should always use single quotes around all strings/scripts until if/when we NEED double quotes and then use double quotes until if/when we NEED no quotes.

I also find associative array definitions clearer if you put the indices inside square brackets and use assignments, like declare -p prints them.

So, I'd do:

$ declare -A prices=( ['apple']='1.99' ['banana']='2.99' ['peanut butter']='4.99' )

$ declare -p prices
declare -A prices=([apple]="1.99" ["peanut butter"]="4.99" [banana]="2.99" )

$ item='peanut butter'

$ price="${prices["$item"]}"; echo "$price"
4.99

and then I KNOW I don't need to even think about potential globbing, word splitting, etc.

Note by the way that it should be echo "$price". not echo $price.
